title: Next Permutation
spaceBreakdown:
- index variables i, j (and swap's internal temp): O(1)
- reverse(): in-place two-pointer, O(1) auxiliary
- no recursion, no containers allocated
- not counted: input vector (modified in place)
approach: The next permutation is the smallest lexicographic increase: find the rightmost index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1] (the suffix after i is non-increasing), swap nums[i] with the rightmost element in the suffix that is larger than it, then reverse that suffix to make it ascending. If no such i exists, the whole array is non-increasing (the last permutation), so reverse it to get the first. This is one forward scan, one backward scan, and one in-place reverse - all O(n), using only index variables.
hints: In [1,2,3]→[1,3,2] only the last two elements changed, but in [2,3,1]→[3,1,2] all three did. What property of the trailing elements decides how far back you must reach to make the smallest possible increase?

Standard next-permutation algorithm: find the rightmost ascent nums[i]<nums[i+1], swap nums[i] with the rightmost element larger than it, then reverse the suffix after i. In [1,2,3]: ascent at i=1 (2<3), swap with j=2 → [1,3,2], reverse suffix [2] → [1,3,2].

```
i = last index with a[i] < a[i+1]
if i >= 0:
    j = last index with a[j] > a[i]
    swap a[i], a[j]
reverse a[i+1 .. n-1]
```

**Single element** - n=1, the only permutation is itself.
`Input: [1]` → `Expected: [1]`
⚠️ Bug: not guarding n<=1 and reading nums[n-2] → out-of-bounds read.

**Fully descending (last permutation)** - no ascent exists anywhere.
`Input: [3,2,1]` → `Expected: [1,2,3]`
⚠️ Bug: skipping the reverse when i<0 → returns [3,2,1].

**Duplicate equal to the pivot in the suffix** - must skip equal values when scanning for j.
`Input: [1,2,1]` → `Expected: [2,1,1]`
⚠️ Bug: using `nums[j] < nums[i]` instead of `nums[j] <= nums[i]` → stops at the equal element, swaps equal values, returns [1,1,2].

**All equal** - no ascent, reverse is a no-op.
`Input: [2,2,2]` → `Expected: [2,2,2]`
⚠️ Bug: using `nums[i] > nums[i+1]` to find the ascent → fails to skip equals, leaves i=1, then the j-scan underflows past index 0.

followUps.q: Find the previous (lexicographically smaller) permutation instead.
followUps.a: Mirror the algorithm: find the rightmost index i where nums[i] > nums[i+1], find the rightmost j>i with nums[j] < nums[i], swap, then reverse the suffix after i. Same O(n) time, O(1) space.

followUps.q: Find the k-th next permutation where k can be up to 10^9.
followUps.a: Repeatedly calling next permutation is O(k·n), too slow. Instead decompose k into a factorial-number-system representation to select each position's element directly from the sorted remaining list, giving O(n^2) time and O(n) space.

followUps.q: Compute the next permutation when only the last m elements fit in memory (m < n).
followUps.a: Run the standard algorithm on the last m elements. If an ascent exists inside the window, the fix is local. If the window is fully non-increasing, the true next permutation requires modifying an element before the window, which is impossible without it - report that the visible suffix is already its last permutation. O(m) time, O(m) space.
